Cause shares are not compared across rule periods in this chapter; that is done only in chapter 9, descriptively.

page_text.main_text_caveat: These correlations describe how the share of electricity customers without power and the share of cell sites out move together across county-reports within a storm. Both may follow the storm's path and strength, so the correlation does not show how much one drives the other.
page_text.lag_pattern: Cell outages line up about as closely with power outages 6 hours earlier (median correlation 0.62) as with power outages at the same time (0.61), and less closely with power outages 24 hours earlier (0.35).
page_text.methods_denominator_note: EAGLE-I's modeled customer count is below EAGLE-I's own recorded outages in 230 of 2,106 storm-counties (for example, Henderson County, North Carolina: 24 modeled customers, 131,460 customers out, 49,494 households). Those storm-counties are left out of every % of customers result; using households as the denominator instead is shown as a sensitivity.
page_text.no_exposure_model: Chapter 6 fits no model that controls for exposure; the plan does not include one.

notes: EAGLE-I 'customers' are electricity meters, not people or households.
EAGLE-I covers 2014-2025, so storms in 2026 (Isaias) have no power match or overlay until a 2026 release exists.
Co-movement is a Spearman rank correlation across county-reports within a storm; it describes how the two move together, not why.
Counties whose EAGLE-I modeled customer count is below EAGLE-I's own recorded outages are left out of % of customers.
Every result carries its count by EAGLE-I coverage flag; low_coverage = the state's minimum covered share below 0.75 that year.

page_text.storm_misses: Here a storm's peak share pools each county's own peak report, so it can differ from the single-report peak in chapter 3. Held out of the fit, with misses of 5 percentage points or more listed, storms' pooled peak shares were higher than predicted for Ida (28.4% observed, 9.1% predicted), Helene (13.5% observed, 8.2% predicted) and Irma (27.0% observed, 17.9% predicted); and lower than predicted for Idalia (2.3% observed, 8.1% predicted), Nicholas (2.5% observed, 15.4% predicted) and Nicole (1.2% observed, 10.0% predicted). Flooding, road access and fiber cuts are possible unmeasured factors; this design cannot tell whether they, or something else, account for the gaps.

notes: Peak share = a county's highest share of sites out across the storm's reports, at its own peak report.

Wind at the nearest track point is the storm's intensity there, not the wind measured in the county.
Calibration is judged on storms held out of the fit, one at a time.

original.headline: In this data, counties with higher social vulnerability did not take measurably longer for cell outages to fall below 5% of sites. The estimates rule out a large delay for the most vulnerable quartile (a rate of recovery more than 10% slower), though they can't rule out a smaller one.
original.headline_bound: For the most vulnerable quartile, the 95% interval for the hazard ratio runs from 0.91 to 1.47: a rate of falling below 5% more than 10% lower than the least vulnerable quartile's is outside it; a smaller shortfall, or a rate up to 47% higher, is not.

page_text.best_case_sensitivity: Sensitivity display, not a finding: if counties that leave the reports while still out are counted as having fallen below 5% at their next unreported report, the third and fourth quartiles reach it sooner (hazard ratios 1.35 [1.07, 1.71] and 1.32 [1.06, 1.65]). The difference disappears if those counties are instead kept at risk to the storm's last report (1.04 [0.84, 1.29] and 1.02 [0.81, 1.29]).
page_text.wording: Associations only: these results describe how long counties in each SVI quartile took to fall below 5% of sites out. They do not show why, and say nothing about anyone's intent.
cannot_rule_out: SVI is correlated with rurality, terrain and network density; any of these, or other differences between counties, may be associated with both SVI and restoration times.
Public DIRS tables combine all providers, so differences between providers' networks in different counties cannot be seen.
Counties that leave the reports while still out are censored; if leaving the reports differs by SVI quartile, the comparison can shift (see the best and worst cases).
Wind zone, distance and track-point wind do not capture flooding, road access or fiber cuts.

notes: Quartiles are of the at-risk storm-counties' SVI 2022 national percentiles; national cut points are a sensitivity display.
Hazard ratios above 1 mean a county reaches below 5% of sites out sooner than the lowest-SVI quartile, holding exposure and storm fixed.
The event is the first report from which a county stays below 5% in every later report that includes it.

page_text.finding: Where the order could be determined (351 of 499 counties, as defined), cell outages fell below 5% first in 158 counties and power outages first in 66; in 127 both fell below 5% in the same report. Where both fell below 5% (296 counties), the median gap is 0 days.

page_text.not_measured: Factors this data doesn't measure, any of which could bear on the order: portable cell sites brought in after the storm, generators placed at cell sites, service carried by other networks (roaming), the order in which crews restore lines and repairs to the network connections that link sites (backhaul).

page_text.finding: In storms from 2022 on, counties served by more mobile providers did not show a consistent difference in how long cell outages took to fall below 5% of sites.
